stem: The student wants to provide an example of an influent stream. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Hydrologists classify streams by the direction water moves between a channel and the groundwater beneath it.
- In an effluent stream, groundwater seeps up into the channel, so flow can continue through dry spells.
- In a losing stream, water seeps down through the streambed into the aquifer below.
- Losing streams are also known as influent streams.
- Sandoval Wash, in an arid basin, carries less water downstream as flow seeps through its gravelly bed.
- Marrow Brook, in a humid valley, is fed by groundwater springs year-round.
choices: Fed by groundwater springs year-round, Marrow Brook is an example of a stream that receives water from the aquifer beneath its channel.
Influent streams, which are also known as losing streams, lose water as it seeps down through their beds into the aquifer below.
Sandoval Wash, which carries less water downstream as flow seeps through its gravelly bed into the aquifer, is a losing stream.
Unlike Marrow Brook, which is fed by groundwater springs, Sandoval Wash lies in an arid basin and has a gravelly streambed.
explanation: The goal asks for an example, so you need one named stream tied to the property 'influent.' The notes use that word only once, to say that losing streams are also called influent streams. So any choice that names a specific stream and shows it is a losing stream gives an example of an influent stream, even if the word 'influent' never appears. Choice C names Sandoval Wash, says its water seeps through its bed into the aquifer, and calls it a losing stream. That is a specific instance clearly linked to the right category.

A.why: You correctly looked for a named stream, but you read 'influent' as 'water flowing in.' The notes define influent streams as losing streams, which send water down into the aquifer. Marrow Brook receives groundwater, which makes it an effluent stream, the opposite category.

B.why: You picked a sentence at the wrong level. It accurately defines influent streams as a category but never names a specific stream, so it gives a generalization instead of an example.

D.why: You chose the right stream but missed that the sentence never links it to the property. It compares Sandoval Wash's setting and streambed with Marrow Brook's but never says that Sandoval Wash loses water to the aquifer, so it never shows that the stream is influent.

stem: The student wants to make a generalization about legume cover crops. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Cover crops are planted between cash-crop seasons to protect and enrich soil.
- Legumes, a plant family that includes clovers and vetches, host bacteria in root nodules that convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form plants can use.
- When legume cover crops are tilled under, that nitrogen becomes available to the next crop.
- Crimson clover, a legume cover crop, grows quickly in mild autumns.
- Hairy vetch, another legume cover crop, can survive winters as cold as −30°C.
- Cereal rye, a non-legume cover crop, adds no new nitrogen but absorbs leftover nitrogen that would otherwise wash away.
choices: Crimson clover and hairy vetch are both legume cover crops, though hairy vetch can survive far colder winters than crimson clover can.
Legume cover crops can survive winters as cold as −30°C, so they can protect soil even in regions with the harshest climates.
Cover crops, which are planted between cash-crop seasons, add nitrogen to the soil that becomes available to the next crop when tilled under.
Legume cover crops enrich soil for the next crop: bacteria in their root nodules capture atmospheric nitrogen, which is released when the plants are tilled under.
explanation: A generalization must make a claim about the whole category, legume cover crops, and that claim must hold for every member the notes describe. The notes give two category-level facts: legumes host nitrogen-converting bacteria in their root nodules, and legume cover crops release that nitrogen to the next crop when they are tilled under. Choice D combines exactly those facts and keeps the plural category noun as its subject. It does not stretch a fact about one member into a claim about the whole group, and it does not slip into the larger category of all cover crops.

A.why: You picked a sentence at the wrong level. It names two specific legume cover crops and compares them, so it is about individual instances, not a claim about legume cover crops as a group.

B.why: You noticed that a generalization needs a broad subject, but this one takes a fact about a single crop and applies it to the whole group. The notes say only that hairy vetch survives −30°C. They say crimson clover grows in mild autumns, so cold hardiness is not a property of all legume cover crops.

C.why: You chose a broad claim but about the wrong category. The goal is about legume cover crops, and this sentence is about all cover crops. The claim is also false for that larger group, because the notes say cereal rye, a cover crop, adds no new nitrogen.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Resistant starch is starch that escapes digestion in the small intestine and is instead fermented by bacteria in the large intestine.
- Cooking and then cooling certain starchy foods raises their resistant starch content.
- In one analysis, potatoes that were cooked and then chilled had about twice the resistant starch of freshly cooked potatoes.
- Green bananas are also rich in resistant starch, but much of it turns to sugar as the fruit ripens.
The student wants to provide an example of a food whose resistant starch content can be increased by how it is prepared.
choices: Cooking and then cooling certain starchy foods raises their resistant starch content, which bacteria later ferment in the large intestine.
Green bananas are rich in resistant starch, though much of that starch turns into sugar as the fruit gradually ripens.
Potatoes that are cooked and then chilled contain about twice as much resistant starch as freshly cooked potatoes do.
Potatoes and green bananas both contain resistant starch, which bacteria ferment in the large intestine rather than the small.
explanation: The goal asks for an example, so you need one named food, and that food has to be linked to an increase that comes from preparation. The goal says "prepared," but the notes say "cooking and then cooling," so you have to see that these mean the same thing here. Choice C names potatoes and shows that cooking and chilling them doubles their resistant starch, so it does both jobs.

A.why: You saw the preparation idea and stopped there. This is a statement about "certain starchy foods" as a group, and it never names a food, so it gives a generalization when the goal asks for an example.

B.why: You found a named food whose resistant starch changes and took that as the property in the goal. But ripening is not preparation, and here the starch goes down, not up. You picked the right level with the wrong property.

D.why: This names potatoes, the right food, but only says they share resistant starch with bananas. Nothing in it shows preparation raising the amount, so the property the goal asks for is missing.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Portolan charts were nautical charts made in the Mediterranean region from the late 1200s onward.
- Most were drawn on a single sheet of vellum.
- Most show coastlines in close detail but leave inland areas nearly blank.
- A web of crisscrossing rhumb lines covers most portolan charts, helping sailors set a compass course.
- The Carta Pisana, from about 1275, is the oldest surviving portolan chart.
The student wants to make a generalization about how portolan charts treated land away from the coast.
choices: The Carta Pisana, the oldest surviving portolan chart, leaves the land beyond its coastlines nearly blank.
All portolan charts left inland areas entirely blank, recording only what sailors could see from the water.
Most portolan charts were covered with rhumb lines, a web of lines that helped sailors set a course.
Most portolan charts depicted coastlines in close detail but left the land beyond them nearly blank.
explanation: A generalization makes a claim about the whole category, and this one has to be about inland areas. Choice D is about portolan charts in general, it is about the land away from the coast, and it keeps the notes' own limits ("most," "nearly blank").

A.why: This has the right content but the wrong level. It makes one chart, the Carta Pisana, its subject, which makes it an example. The notes also never say how that particular chart treats inland areas.

B.why: You knew a generalization makes a broad claim, and "all" looked like the strongest version. But the notes say "most" and "nearly blank," and this choice turns that into "all" and "entirely blank." The last clause adds a reason the notes never give.

C.why: This is at the right level, since it is a claim about most portolan charts, but it is about rhumb lines, not land away from the coast. Hitting the right level does not count if the topic is wrong.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- In resist dyeing, part of a cloth is blocked so that dye cannot reach it, leaving a pattern.
- Javanese batik uses hot wax brushed or drawn onto the cloth as the resist.
- Yoruba artisans in Nigeria make adire eleko by painting a paste of cassava starch onto cloth.
- In Japanese shibori, the cloth is folded, twisted, or tightly bound with thread before it is dyed.
The student wants to provide an example of a resist-dyeing technique that does not rely on applying any substance to the cloth.
choices: Some resist-dyeing techniques protect parts of a cloth by manipulating the fabric itself rather than coating its surface.
In Japanese shibori, cloth is folded, twisted, or bound with thread before dyeing, so the fabric itself blocks the dye.
To make adire eleko, Yoruba artisans paint cloth with cassava paste, a resist made from starch rather than from wax.
Like Javanese batik, Japanese shibori is a resist-dyeing technique in which part of the cloth is blocked from the dye.
explanation: The goal asks for one named technique, and that technique has to work without applying anything to the cloth. The notes never use that wording. You have to work out that folding, twisting, and binding change the cloth without adding anything to it. Choice B names shibori and gives that method, so it supplies both the instance and the property.

A.why: This states the right property, but only for "some techniques" in general. No technique is named, so it is a generalization where the goal asks for an example.

C.why: "Rather than from wax" reads like the contrast the goal wants. But cassava paste is still a substance painted onto the cloth, so adire eleko is an example of exactly what the goal rules out.

D.why: This names shibori, the correct technique, so it is easy to stop here. But it only calls shibori a resist technique like batik and never says how it works. The property that sets it apart from batik is missing.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- A gaining stream takes in water from the surrounding groundwater.
- A losing stream leaks water downward into the ground beneath its channel.
- Losing streams occur mostly in arid regions, where the water table lies below the streambed.
- Corvo Creek, a losing stream in an arid basin, flows over a water table about 30 meters below its bed.
- Along one 12-kilometer reach, Corvo Creek loses roughly a third of its flow.
The student wants to make a generalization about where losing streams occur.
choices: Losing streams occur mostly in arid regions, where the water table lies below the level of the streambed.
Corvo Creek, a losing stream in an arid basin, flows over a water table about 30 meters below its bed.
Every stream that flows through an arid region leaks water into the ground beneath its channel.
Whereas gaining streams take in groundwater, losing streams leak water into the ground below them.
explanation: The goal asks for a claim about losing streams as a group, and the claim has to be about where they occur. Choice A makes losing streams in general its subject, says where they are found (arid regions with a low water table), and keeps the notes' limit ("mostly").

B.why: This choice covers the right topic, since it says where a losing stream is found, and even uses the arid basin and the low water table. But its subject is one stream, Corvo Creek, so it is an example, not a generalization.

C.why: This one is general, but it switches the subject to arid-region streams and claims that every one of them loses water. The notes only say that losing streams are mostly found in arid regions, not that all streams there lose water.

D.why: This makes a broad claim and marks a contrast, but it explains what losing streams are, not where they occur. The goal names location, and this choice never mentions it.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- A keystone species has an effect on its ecosystem out of proportion to its abundance.
- Ecologist Robert Paine identified the ochre sea star, which preys on mussels, as a keystone species.
- In Paine's tide-pool plots in Washington State, mussels far outnumbered sea stars.
- When Paine removed the sea stars, mussels spread and the number of species in the plots fell sharply.
- Sea otters, which eat sea urchins, are another often-cited keystone species.
The student wants to provide an example of a species whose influence on its ecosystem far exceeds what its numbers would suggest.
choices: A keystone species is one whose effect on its ecosystem is out of proportion to how abundant that species is.
Mussels far outnumbered other animals in Paine's tide pools and spread through the plots once sea stars were gone.
Sea otters and ochre sea stars are both predators, with the otters eating urchins and the sea stars eating mussels.
Removing the ochre sea star, a keystone species, caused the number of species in Paine's tide pools to fall sharply.
explanation: The goal describes the property in its own words: influence far greater than the species' numbers. The notes call that property "keystone." Choice D names one species, the ochre sea star, calls it a keystone species, and shows its large effect. That gives both the instance and the property.

A.why: This is the property the goal describes, but as a definition. It never names a species, so it is a generalization where the goal asks for an example.

B.why: This names a species with a big effect, so it can look right. But mussels were the most numerous animals in the plots, so their effect matches their numbers. They are the opposite of the property the goal asks for.

C.why: This names the right species, but it only describes a trait the two share: both are predators. It never shows either one having an effect larger than its numbers would suggest.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- A ground bass is a short bass line repeated many times while the upper parts change above it.
- Composers of the Baroque era (about 1600–1750) used the technique widely.
- Henry Purcell's aria "Dido's Lament" (1689) is built on a five-bar ground.
- Johann Pachelbel's Canon in D repeats a two-bar bass line 28 times.
The student wants to make a generalization about the structure of pieces built on a ground bass.
choices: Whereas Pachelbel's Canon in D repeats a two-bar bass line, Purcell's "Dido's Lament" is built on a five-bar one.
Pieces built on a ground bass repeat a short bass line many times while the upper parts change above it.
Pachelbel's Canon in D, a well-known Baroque work, sounds its two-bar bass line 28 times in succession.
Most works by Baroque composers, who used the technique widely, were built on a repeating ground bass.
explanation: A generalization about structure has to make ground-bass pieces as a group its subject and describe how they are built. Choice B does that: a short bass line repeats while the parts above it change. It names no single piece.

A.why: This is about structure, but it compares two particular pieces. Comparing two examples is not a claim about the whole category.

C.why: This shows the structure clearly, but through one work. When a single piece is the subject, you have an example, not a generalization.

D.why: "Most" sounded like the signal word for a generalization. But the notes say only that Baroque composers used the technique "widely," not that most of their works used it. This choice also describes how common the technique was, not how the pieces are built.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Brood parasites lay their eggs in the nests of other birds, which then raise the chicks.
- Obligate brood parasites never build nests or rear young of their own.
- The common cuckoo is an obligate brood parasite; its hosts include reed warblers.
- The redhead duck is a facultative brood parasite: females often lay eggs in other ducks' nests but also raise broods of their own.
The student wants to provide an example of a bird that depends entirely on other species to raise its young.
choices: The common cuckoo, an obligate brood parasite, leaves its eggs for hosts such as reed warblers to raise.
Obligate brood parasites never build nests or rear young of their own, relying on host birds instead.
The common cuckoo and the redhead duck both lay eggs in the nests of other birds, which raise the chicks.
The redhead duck, a brood parasite, never builds a nest or raises a brood of young of its own.
explanation: The goal's word "entirely" matches the notes' term "obligate." So you need one named bird that is called an obligate brood parasite. Choice A names the common cuckoo, calls it obligate, and shows hosts raising its young.

B.why: This describes total dependence correctly, but for obligate brood parasites as a group. It never names a bird, so it is a generalization when the goal asks for an example.

C.why: This names the cuckoo, but it puts it next to the redhead duck and states only what the two share: laying eggs in other birds' nests. That fits partial dependence, so it never shows the cuckoo relying on others "entirely."

D.why: This has the shape of a correct example, with a named bird and the total-dependence property. But the notes say redhead females also raise broods of their own, so the claim reverses what the notes say.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
- Hot Jupiters are gas giant exoplanets that orbit very close to their stars.
- Most complete an orbit in fewer than ten days.
- Their size and closeness make them tug noticeably on their stars, so they are relatively easy to detect.
- Only about 1 percent of Sun-like stars appear to host one.
- 51 Pegasi b, a hot Jupiter that orbits every 4.2 days, was the first exoplanet found around a Sun-like star.
The student wants to make a generalization about how readily hot Jupiters can be detected.
choices: 51 Pegasi b, a hot Jupiter that orbits its star every 4.2 days, was the first exoplanet found around a Sun-like star.
Most hot Jupiters, gas giants that orbit very close to their stars, complete a full orbit in fewer than ten days.
Hot Jupiters are relatively easy to detect, since their size and closeness make them tug noticeably on their stars.
Hot Jupiters are easy to detect because they orbit about 1 percent of Sun-like stars, more than any other planet type.
explanation: The goal asks for a claim about hot Jupiters as a group, and the claim has to be about how easily they are detected. Choice C makes the whole category its subject, says they are relatively easy to detect, and gives the reason from the notes.

A.why: Being the first one found does suggest that hot Jupiters are easy to spot. But this choice is about one planet, 51 Pegasi b, so it is an example, and it never makes a claim about detection.

B.why: This uses "most" and the plural category, so it is at the right level. But it is about how long their orbits take, not how readily they can be detected.

D.why: This is about detection, but its reason is not in the notes. The notes give 1 percent to show that hot Jupiters are rare, and they never say they are more common than other planet types or that how common they are affects detection.
